listen_text: Section. Constructive Reasoning. In contrast to extensions of classical logic by modal operators or second-order quantifiers, intuitionistic logic is “non-classical” in that it restricts classical logic. Classical logic is non-constructive in various ways. Intuitionistic logic is intended to capture a more “constructive” kind of reasoning characteristic of a kind of constructive mathematics. The following examples may serve to illustrate some of the underlying motivations. Suppose someone claimed that they had determined a natural number n with the property that if n is even, the Riemann hypothesis is true, and if n is odd, the Riemann hypothesis is false. Great news! Whether the Riemann hypothesis is true or not is one of the big open questions of mathematics, and they seem to have reduced the problem to one of calculation, that is, to the determination of whether a specific number is even or not. What is the magic value of n ? They describe it as follows: n is the natural number that is equal to two if the Riemann hypothesis is true, and three otherwise. Angrily, you demand your money back. From a classical point of view, the description above does in fact determine a unique value of n ; but what you really want is a value of n that is given explicitly. To take another, perhaps less contrived example, consider the following question. We know that it is possible to raise an irrational number to a rational power, and get a rational result. For example, the square of the square root of two equals two . What is less clear is whether or not it is possible to raise an irrational number to an irrational power, and get a rational result. The following theorem answers this in the affirmative: Theorem. There are irrational numbers a and b such that a raised to the power b is rational. End theorem. Proof. Consider the square root of two raised to the square root of two . If this is rational, we are done: we can let a and b both equal the square root of two . Otherwise, it is irrational. Then we have Displayed expression. the square root of two raised to the square root of two, all raised to the square root of two, equals the square root of two raised to the product of two square roots of two, equals the square of the square root of two, equals two. End displayed expression. which is rational. So, in this case, let a be the square root of two raised to the square root of two , and let b be the square root of two . End proof. Does this constitute a valid proof? Most mathematicians feel that it does. But again, there is something a little bit unsatisfying here: we have proved the existence of a pair of real numbers with a certain property, without being able to say which pair of numbers it is. It is possible to prove the same result, but in such a way that the pair a , b is given in the proof: take a equals the square root of three and b equals the logarithm base three of four . Then Displayed expression. a raised to b equals the square root of three raised to the logarithm base three of four, equals three raised to one half times that logarithm, equals three raised to that logarithm and then to the one-half power, equals four to the one-half power, equals two. End displayed expression. since three raised to the logarithm base three of x equals x . Intuitionistic logic is designed to capture a kind of reasoning where moves like the one in the first proof are disallowed. Proving the existence of an x satisfying A of x means that you have to give a specific x , and a proof that it satisfies A , like in the second proof. Proving that A or B holds requires that you can prove one or the other. Formally speaking, intuitionistic logic is what you get if you restrict a derivation system for classical logic in a certain way. From the mathematical point of view, these are just formal deductive systems, but, as already noted, they are intended to capture a kind of mathematical reasoning. One can take this to be the kind of reasoning that is justified on a certain philosophical view of mathematics (such as Brouwer's intuitionism); one can take it to be a kind of mathematical reasoning which is more “concrete” and satisfying (along the lines of Bishop's constructivism); and one can argue about whether or not the formal description captures the informal motivation. But whatever philosophical positions we may hold, we can study intuitionistic logic as a formally presented logic; and for whatever reasons, many mathematical logicians find it interesting to do so. End section.

listen_text: Section. Syntax of Intuitionistic Logic. The syntax of intuitionistic logic is the same as that for propositional logic. In classical propositional logic it is possible to define connectives by others, for example, one can define if A, then B by not A or B , or A or B by not both not A and not B . Thus, presentations of classical logic often introduce some connectives as abbreviations for these definitions. This is not so in intuitionistic logic, with two exceptions: not A can be—and often is—defined as an abbreviation for if A, then falsity . Then, of course, falsity must not itself be defined! Also, A if and only if B can be defined, as in classical logic, as the conditional from A to B and the conditional from B to A . Formulas of propositional intuitionistic logic are built up from propositional variables and the propositional constant falsity using logical connectives. We have: List. Next item. The propositional constant for falsity falsity . Next item. The logical connectives: conjunction (conjunction), disjunction (disjunction), conditional (conditional) Next item. Punctuation marks: (, ), and the comma. End list. Definition. Formula. The set the set of formulas of language L subscript zero of formulas of propositional intuitionistic logic is defined inductively as follows: List. Next item. falsity is an atomic formula. Next item. Every propositional variable propositional variable p subscript i is an atomic formula. Next item. If A and B are formulas, then A and B, enclosed in parentheses is a formula. Next item. If A and B are formulas, then A or B, enclosed in parentheses is a formula. Next item. If A and B are formulas, then the conditional from A to B, enclosed in parentheses is a formula. Next item. Nothing else is a formula. End list. End definition. In addition to the primitive connectives introduced above, we also use the following defined symbols: negation (negation) and biconditional (biconditional). Formulas constructed using the defined operators are to be understood as follows: List. Next item. not A abbreviates if A, then falsity . Next item. A if and only if B abbreviates the conditional from A to B and the conditional from B to A . End list. Although negation is officially treated as an abbreviation, we will sometimes give explicit rules and clauses in definitions for negation as if it were primitive. This is mostly so we can state practice problems. End section.

Proofs of validity of intuitionistic propositions using the BHK interpretation are confusing; they have to be explained better. End editorial note. There is an informal constructive interpretation of the intuitionist connectives, usually known as the Brouwer—Heyting—Kolmogorov interpretation. It uses the notion of a “construction,” which you may think of as a constructive proof. (We don't use “proof” in the BHK interpretation so as not to get confused with the notion of a derivation in a formal derivation system.) Based on this intuitive notion, the BHK interpretation explains the meanings of the intuitionistic connectives. List. Next item. We assume that we know what constitutes a construction of an atomic statement. Next item. A construction of A subscript one and A subscript two is a pair the ordered pair M subscript one, M subscript two where M subscript one is a construction of A subscript one and M subscript two is a construction of A subscript two . Next item. A construction of A subscript one or A subscript two is a pair the ordered pair s, M where s is one and M is a construction of A subscript one , or s is two and M is a construction of A subscript two . Next item. A construction of if A, then B is a function that converts a construction of A into a construction of B . Next item. There is no construction for falsity (absurdity). Next item. not A is defined as synonym for if A, then falsity . That is, a construction of not A is a function converting a construction of A into a construction of falsity . End list. Example. Take not falsity for example. A construction of it is a function which, given any construction of falsity as input, provides a construction of falsity as output. Obviously, the identity function the identity function is such a construction: given a construction M of falsity , the identity function applied to M equals M yields a construction of falsity . End example. Generally speaking, not A means “A construction of A is impossible”. Example. We can prove it for some specific A (for example, falsity or not falsity ), but not in general. Luckily, there are better derivation systems for intuitionistic logic, and more precise semantic interpretations. End section.

listen_text: Section. Natural Deduction. Natural deduction without the classical contradiction rules is a standard derivation system for intuitionistic logic. We repeat the rules here and indicate the motivation using the BHK interpretation. In each case, we can think of a rule which allows us to conclude that if the premises have constructions, so does the conclusion. Since natural deduction derivations have undischarged assumptions, we should consider such a derivation, say, of A from undischarged assumptions Gamma , as a function that turns constructions of all B belongs to Gamma into a construction of A . If there is a derivation of A from no undischarged assumptions, then there is a construction of A in the sense of the BHK interpretation. For the purpose of the discussion, however, we'll suppress the Gamma when not needed. An assumption A by itself is a derivation of A from the undischarged assumption A . This agrees with the BHK-interpretation: the identity function on constructions turns any construction of A into a construction of A . Section. Conjunction. Proof tree. Conjunction introduction rule. listen_text: Section. Axiomatic Derivations. Axiomatic derivations for intuitionistic propositional logic are the conceptually simplest, and historically first, derivation systems. They work just as in classical propositional logic. Definition. Derivability. If Gamma is a set of formulas of language L then a derivation from Gamma is a finite sequence A subscript one , and so on, A subscript n of formulas where for each i is at most n one of the following holds: List. Next item. A subscript i belongs to Gamma ; or Next item. A subscript i is an axiom; or Next item. A subscript i follows from some A subscript j and A subscript k with j is less than i and k is less than i by modus ponens, that is, A subscript k is syntactically identical to the conditional from A subscript j to A subscript i . End list. End definition. Definition. Axioms. The set of P A X of axioms for the intuitionistic propositional logic are all formulas of the following forms: Displayed expression. Nine intuitionistic axiom forms. One: if A and B, then A. Two: if A and B, then B. Three: if A, then if B, then A and B. Four: if A, then A or B. Five: if A, then B or A. Six: if A implies C, then if B implies C, then A or B implies C. Seven: if A, then if B, then A. Eight: if A implies that B implies C, then if A implies B, then A implies C. Nine: if falsity, then A. End axiom forms. End displayed expression. End definition. Definition. Derivability. A formula A is derivable from Gamma , written A is derivable from Gamma , if there is a derivation from Gamma ending in A . End definition. Definition. Theorems. A formula A is a theorem if there is a derivation of A from the empty set. We write A is derivable without assumptions if A is a theorem and A is not derivable without assumptions if it is not. End definition. Proposition. If A is derivable from Gamma in the axiomatic derivation system for intuitionistic logic, A is derivable from Gamma also in classical logic. In particular, if A is an intuitionistic theorem, it is also a classical theorem. End proposition. Proof. Every intuitionistic axiom is also a classical axiom, so every derivation in intuitionistic logic is also a derivation in classical logic. End proof. End section. End chapter.
